t: Count Nodes With the Highest Score — Every Score in One Bottom-Up Pass
o: We get a binary tree as a parents array (parents[0] = -1 marks the root). Deleting a node v and its edges splits the tree into components: one subtree under each child of v, plus — unless v is the root — the component above v containing the remaining n - size(v) nodes. The score of v is the product of those sizes, and we must count how many nodes attain the maximum. In Example 1, leaves 3 and 4 each score 4 (everything else stays connected), node 1 scores 4, the root scores 3 x 1 = 3, so the maximum 4 is achieved by three nodes. In Example 2, nodes 0 and 1 both score 2 while node 2 scores 1 x 1 = 1. With n up to 100000, recomputing components per node is hopeless; instead compute every subtree size once bottom-up, since the component sizes around v are exactly its children's subtree sizes together with n - size(v).
k: Removing v yields components whose sizes are each child's subtree size, plus n - size(v) when v is not the root.
One post-order accumulation of subtree sizes makes every score computable in O(1) extra work per node — O(n) total.
Scores reach roughly (n/3)^3 ≈ 3.7e13 for n = 100000, overflowing 32-bit integers: use 64-bit products.

a.i: Build children adjacency lists from the parents array. A DFS returns each node's subtree size to its parent; while unwinding, multiply the children's sizes together, also multiplying by n - own size for non-root nodes, and maintain the running maximum score with the number of nodes realizing it.
s: DFS from the root; each call returns its subtree size.
Multiply child sizes into the node's score; multiply by n - size too if the node is not the root.
Update the global maximum and its multiplicity.
Return the multiplicity after the traversal.
a.t: O(n) — each node is visited once with O(1) arithmetic per visit.
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency lists plus recursion depth up to n on a path-shaped tree.

a.n: Approach 2: Iterative Sweep in Reverse BFS Order
a.i: Recursion depth can hit n on degenerate trees. Instead list the nodes in breadth-first order from the root, then sweep that list backwards: by the time a node is reached, all its descendants have already finalized their subtree sizes, which were accumulated upward, so no call stack is needed.
s: Build children lists and record nodes in BFS order starting at the root.
For each node, sum children's finished sizes and multiply them into its score.
Include the factor n - size for non-root nodes; update max and count.
Store the finished size for the node's parent to consume later.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to lay out the BFS order and one reverse pass to accumulate sizes.
a.sp: O(n) — children lists, the order array and the size array.

w: Describe the DFS version conceptually, then switch to the reversed-BFS implementation whenever recursion depth is a concern — it is the safer default in Python. Pitfalls: 32-bit overflow on the product, forgetting the upper component n - size(v) for non-root nodes, and counting a leaf's score wrong (it is always n - 1). Note the root never has an upper factor, and internal nodes with two big subtrees tend to lose. Follow-ups: report the actual winning nodes (keep a list beside the counter), or generalize to k-ary trees — nothing structural changes.
